H adds C–D (only in H, teal). The union keeps all four nodes and all four edges, each in the color of the graph it came from." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. Nodes with the same ID are merged, whatever their labels; where both graphs give the same node (or edge) a label, attribute, or weight, this graph's value takes precedence and the other graph fills in the rest. Duplicate edges are not added. Two edges count as the same edge when they join the same pair of node IDs (in the same direction, for directed graphs). Union is the operation to reach for when two graphs describe parts of the same network and you want everything in one place, for example: - combining snapshots of a network taken at different times - merging edges from several data sources (e.g., interactions reported by different experiments) over a shared set of node IDs - overlaying one relationship type on another, such as "works with" and "emails" Because nodes are matched by ID, the two graphs must use a shared numbering for the same entities. If the numbering differs, use `disjoint_union()` (to keep everything separate) or rebuild one graph with matching IDs first. Isolated nodes from both graphs are kept. Edges from this graph keep their IDs; edges only `other` has get fresh IDs above every ID this graph has used. Neither input graph is modified. To let the other graph's values win instead, use `compose()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to union with. It must have the same directedness as this graph. Its nodes are matched to this graph's nodes by ID; nodes and edges it has that this graph lacks are added, and for nodes and edges present in both, its labels, attributes, and weights are used only where this graph has no value of its own. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. It is weighted if either input is weighted. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness (one directed, one undirected), or if the same label belongs to different node IDs in the two graphs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Union takes the pointwise superset of nodes and edges, merging any nodes that share an ID; where attributes clash, the calling graph wins. Both operands must agree on directedness, because there is no principled way to fold a directed edge into an undirected graph without losing information. If either operand is weighted, so is the result. Use `disjoint_union()` when you want to keep node IDs strictly separate. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes are matched by **ID**, not by label. Here both graphs number their nodes 1, 2, 3; `g2` adds an edge between nodes 2 and 3 that `g1` lacks, so the union has all three nodes and both edges: ::: {#4ce9703d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g1.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g1.add_edge("A", "B") g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g2.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g2.add_edge("B", "C") result = g1.union(g2) result.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#d8840244 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: This makes union a natural way to combine two snapshots of the same network taken at different times, folding in whatever new nodes or edges appeared: ::: {#ec3dc743 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} t1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) t1.add_path_graph(3) # 1-2-3 t2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): t2.add_node() t2.add_edge(1, 3) # a new direct connection combined = t1.union(t2) combined.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: When both graphs describe the same node or edge, this graph's values win and the other graph only fills gaps. Node "A" keeps `team="red"` from `g1` but gains `city="Oslo"` from `g2`, and the shared edge keeps `g1`'s weight of `1.0`: ::: {#71a21eae .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g1.add_node(label="A", team="red") g1.add_node(label="B") g1.add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.0) g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g2.add_node(label="A", team="blue", city="Oslo") g2.add_node(label="B") g2.add_node(label="C") g2.add_edge("A", "B", weight=5.0) g2.add_edge("B", "C") merged = g1.union(g2) merged.get_node_df().select("label", "team", "city") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
